chapter: Later years and the club's fate
title: Meeting Lizzie Miles and bringing her to the club
summary: How Sid met Lizzie Miles through a radio interview and put her on stage; her career afterwards.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: And he's just, uh, great. Yes, great. But that seems to be the thing now I see with, uh, for popularity. So we're getting back to, it's not folk music and it's not completely blues, but it is a, I believe it's sort of a combination of folk, rhythm, and blues. The style that's evolving now, or gelling, you know, which would be popular for a while. And I hate to think what the next one will be, I don't know. But Lizzy was here, Lizzy Miles, she, um, I met Lizzy on a radio interview. Tony Almericka used to have a band in town, and, uh, he was a disc jockey. So, uh, we played Dixieland music and he was a big advocate of Dixieland jazz. And we had a place called, uh, Parisian Room, and he had jazz concerts on a Sunday afternoon. And he was one of the guys actually, uh, instrumental in the big Dixieland revival because, and then he got a line up for nationwide broadcast right from there, you see. And Fazola, probably the world's greatest blues clarinet player, had come to town and Fazola was playing with him. And, uh, so he got a little, uh, radio program and, uh, uh, I was up for an interview with Shawke and some other guys one day. And I met Lizzy Miles, who used to continually write letters to Tony Almericka about his misinformation. You got the years wrong. It wasn't 1927 and it wasn't Bessie Smith. So I happened to be up there one day and here comes Lizzy Miles, dressed 1924 style, with a parlor record set. Well, believe me, it must have been worth a hundred dollars a piece collector's items. And Lizzy set him straight and we got to talking over there. And, uh, I felt that Lizzy should be on before the people. She wasn't singing. She was a washerwoman. She had gotten out of her business fifteen to twenty years. And, uh, we put Lizzy on the street with a piano player, on the stage with a piano player. And she began singing these songs, many songs in French. And Lizzy went on to make a lot of records and make some good appearances. She did national television, NBC, I think, national television. She played some of the bigger clubs in the country. And she always came back here because she was a religious woman and she had taken some kind of a vow many years ago that she wouldn't appear on the stage if something were granted her. So she, uh, she made a distinction between a bandstand and a stage and she got up there easy. And she was a little bit of a band. But she was a wonderful one.
